conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I’m Dr. Lee, one of the surgical team. You’ve been admitted because of worsening hand ischemia from your right arm dialysis fistula. We’re here to help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, yes, my hand’s been cold and numb, especially when I use it. It’s getting worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s called steal syndrome. The fistula is pulling too much blood away from your hand. We’re planning a procedure called fistula banding to reduce the flow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that affect my dialysis? I need that fistula to work.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good question. We’ll narrow the fistula just enough to restore blood to your hand while keeping it usable for dialysis. There’s a small risk it could clot, but saving your hand comes first.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. When will this happen?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Later today. First, we’ll get you prepped and review the consent. You’ll have hemodialysis first, as scheduled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I had dialysis this morning already. Is that okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that was outpatient. Today’s session will be after your procedure, to keep your fluids and electrolytes balanced.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my warfarin? I’m on blood thinners.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve held your warfarin temporarily to reduce bleeding risk during surgery. We’ll restart it soon after, once we’re sure there’s no bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I was worried about clots with my history.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We know. That’s why we’re being careful. You’ll get heparin shots while off warfarin to prevent clots.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re back from the procedure. The banding was successful. We narrowed the fistula, and your radial pulse is now strong.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How does my hand feel? It still feels cold.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a good sign it’s still cold right now—means we reduced the flow enough. It should warm up over the next few hours as circulation adjusts.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the pain? It aches a bit.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll give you Vicodin for pain. Keep your arm elevated on pillows to reduce swelling.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just checking in. How’s the pain now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better, since I took the medicine. My hand feels a little warmer too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great progress. You’ll have dialysis in a few hours. We’ll monitor your potassium and fluids closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You finished dialysis well. Your vitals are stable, and labs look good. No signs of infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. Should I still take my other meds like mirtazapine and quetiapine?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ve continued all your regular medications except warfarin, which we’ll restart tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. Your hand is warmer, and the pulse is strong. We’re going to restart warfarin at a lower dose today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is the fistula still working? I feel a buzz, but is that normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the buzzing is a good sign—means blood is flowing. We checked with ultrasound; the fistula is open and functioning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. What about my other arm? I have a fistula there too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Both fistulas are intact. For dialysis, they’ll use the right one to pull blood and the left to return it—‘1 and 1’ setup.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your INR is starting to rise, which means the warfarin is working. We’ll keep monitoring it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my lupus and kidney issues? Are they stable?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your lupus is quiet, and your dialysis is managing your kidney failure well. The main issue was the hand ischemia, which we’ve addressed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow morning if everything stays stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What should I watch for at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep an eye on your hand. If it turns cold, blue, or you can’t move it, call us. Also watch for fever, pus, or heavy bleeding from the site.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the dressing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep it dry for two days. After that, you can remove it and shower. Steri-strips will fall off on their own.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Pain medicine? I still have some ache.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll go home with hydrocodone for a few days. Don’t take it longer than three days unless we say so. It can cause constipation—so we’re adding docusate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, and when do I see the surgeon again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: In about two weeks. Call the office to schedule. Also, weigh yourself daily—call if you gain more than three pounds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re cleared to go home. You’re alert, pain is controlled, and your hand is warm with good pulses.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Remember: no lifting over 10 pounds for three days, no heavy exercise for two weeks, and start fistula exercises in a week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And no blood pressure checks or IVs in the access arm.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. You’ve got it. Call us with any concerns. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will go over your prescriptions and discharge instructions one more time before you leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ve got my pills and the instructions. I’ll follow up soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re officially discharged. Safe travels home.
